clue.text: Good time to restrain American Air Force

indicators.note: to restrain something is to hold it in, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
T is the usual abbreviation for time
US stands for the United States, so American

explanation.surface: A good spell keeping the American Air Force on the ground or out of trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air Force' reads as the military service, but here it is the definition read literally: a force of air.
explanation.definitionFit: A gust is a sudden strong rush of wind, literally a force exerted by moving air.

indicators.note: only a little of the word is wanted, so just its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
a rasp is a coarse file for shaping wood or metal

explanation.surface: An instruction to look at a small government dossier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'file' suggests paperwork, but it is the metalworking tool.
explanation.definitionFit: To see in the sense of understanding an idea is to take it in mentally, as in 'I see what you mean'.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: utterly exhausted, informal British usage
second meaning: smashed into many pieces

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one description of a worn-out person; the two halves are separate senses of a single word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is informal slang for complete exhaustion and also literally describes glass smashed into fragments.

clue.text: Marcel Marceau seemingly such a green activist?

definitions.text: Marcel Marceau seemingly such a green activist?

parts.note: surface reading: the French mime looks as if he is clasping something in his arms
setter's reading: an environmentalist nicknamed for embracing trunks in the forest

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the great French mime was secretly an environmental campaigner.
explanation.walkthrough: Marcel Marceau was a famous French mime; a mime embracing an invisible trunk would look like the slang term for an eco-campaigner.
explanation.definitionFit: The hyphenated term is a jokey or dismissive label for a passionate environmentalist, from protesters embracing forest trunks.

clue.text: Mac artist at home with paint

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist
someone at home is in
a coat is a layer of paint

explanation.surface: A painter on a Mac computer, working from home on a picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mac artist' suggests digital art on an Apple computer; Mac is the definition, short for mackintosh.
explanation.definitionFit: A mac, short for mackintosh, is the British word for a waterproof outer garment worn in wet weather.

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped
in a down clue, sending something up makes it read from bottom to top

parts.note: a mate is a partner, here without its last letter

explanation.surface: Fooling a friend by mocking them relentlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent up' sounds like mockery, but in a down entry it means written upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To trap someone by trickery is to deceive them into a compromising position, a close synonym.

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or not in place, so the letters get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A spotless Lulu, the Scottish pop singer, going out for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Lulu is a Scottish pop singer, which makes the surface read like celebrity gossip.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something spotless and pure, without any stain or blemish, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Journey on goods vehicle in Glasgow district

parts.note: to go is to journey
a van carries goods

explanation.surface: Travelling by delivery van through part of Glasgow.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'on' means placed above, so the journey sits atop the vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Govan is an area of Glasgow on the south bank of the Clyde, known for shipbuilding.

parts.note: a runner is a long narrow rug for a hall or stairs
something lifted is up

explanation.surface: Thin rugs raised off the floor in a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seconds' looks like a brief time, but it means those who finish second.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who come second in a contest are the people placed just behind the winner; the question mark flags the plural sense.

clue.text: Spots an East End carriage reportedly?

indicators.note: reportedly means as said by others, so the sound counts, not the spelling

parts.note: a hackney carriage, with the H dropped as a Cockney would

explanation.surface: Seeing a horse-drawn cab in London's East End.
explanation.walkthrough: East End Cockneys traditionally drop the H, so a hackney carriage becomes 'an 'ackney'; a hackney carriage is an old term for a cab.
explanation.definitionFit: Acne is a skin condition producing pimples, which are commonly called spots in Britain.

parts.note: taken as written
arch means chief or principal, as in archenemy
first is written 1st, and 1 looks like I

explanation.surface: Something significant happening for the first time on behalf of a rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is reading the numeral in 1st as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A subversive is someone working to undermine authority, and one who rejects all government fits that description.

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
equal scores are even

explanation.surface: Every dwarf being little and on a level footing.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition counts the dwarfs of the Snow White fairy tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow White's companions number exactly that many, so the figure stands for the whole group.

clue.text: Course taken by European film company

parts.note: a path is a course or route
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A European movie studio choosing a particular route.
explanation.walkthrough: Pathé is a long-established French studio, famous in Britain for its newsreels.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathé is a French producer and distributor of movies, one of the oldest such businesses in the world.

clue.text: Check name in claim for dispute

parts.note: CH is the chess abbreviation for check

indicators.note: one thing placed inside another means it sits within the second's letters

parts.note: to allege is to claim
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Verifying a name on an insurance claim before contesting it.
explanation.walkthrough: CH is chess notation for check; the abbreviation for name goes inside the claim, which then follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispute something is to call it into question, which is exactly what a formal objection does; both work as verbs.

clue.text: 10 Across, no saint, deceptive Persian enemy?

indicators.note: something deceptive is not what it seems, so the letters are disguised in a new order
no means without, so the following letter is removed

parts.note: the answer to 10 Across
S is the abbreviation for saint, and it is taken out

explanation.surface: A rebel who is no saint, a treacherous foe of Persia.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the single letter for saint goes, not ST; the remaining eight letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Thracians from the ancient Balkans fought against Persian invaders, so one could be an opponent; the question mark admits the definition by example.

indicators.note: a mischievous thing plays tricks and misbehaves, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Enthusiastically taking a liking to a naughty explorer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mischievous' is both the anagram signal and an apt description of the boy hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Twain's boy hero has many escapades along the Mississippi, so he is a fictional adventurer.

indicators.note: something that failed has fallen apart, so these letters are rebuilt in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A French recipe that was a hopeless effort and flopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost cause' reads as part of the story of a kitchen disaster, but its nine letters are exactly the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassoulet is a slow-cooked stew of beans and meats from south-west France, a classic regional recipe.

clue.text: Four from Rome in vessels for turns

indicators.note: placed inside means one set of letters sits within another

parts.note: pots are vessels
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A Roman quartet tucked into ships, ready to change direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessels' suggests ships, but these are containers for cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: To pivot is to rotate on a fixed point, so the plural verb matches turning movements.

indicators.note: something on the outside wraps around what is within it

parts.note: a marked difference is an obvious one
taken as written
L is a learner, from the L-plate on British learner cars

explanation.surface: A clueless student who was graded only on the outside of the work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'marked' reads as graded, but it means noticeable.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unaware of what is going on around them is unknowing, a close synonym of the adjective.

clue.text: Where one goes after class tracked location?

definitions.text: Where one goes after class tracked location?

parts.note: surface reading: where students head when lessons end
setter's reading: a place on the railway tracks, a big London terminus that commuters pass through on the way home

explanation.surface: Tracing where a pupil goes once school is out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tracked' sounds like following someone, but it means served by rails: the place is a mainline London station.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterloo is one of London's busiest railway terminals, a rail location that many commuters use going home.

indicators.note: bats is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Flying bats find the Gorgon entertaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like the animals but is the British slang adjective meaning mad.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this Gorgon had living serpents for hair and turned onlookers to stone.

clue.text: Boys circling northern edge fall from cliff

indicators.note: to circle something is to go all round it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: lads are boys
N is the abbreviation for northern
a lip is an edge or rim

explanation.surface: Boys walking round the northern rim watching a tumble from the cliff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fall from cliff' is the definition; landslip is the usual British word for what Americans call a landslide.
explanation.definitionFit: A collapse of earth and rock down a slope is the same as a cliff fall, the British word for a landslide.

clue.text: Lad I'm with, not all there: thicko

indicators.note: not all of the words are used, only a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone admitting the boy they are with is a bit slow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not all there' doubles as an idiom for being stupid, which suits the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A thicko is British slang for a stupid person, and so is the answer; both are informal insults.

parts.note: an author is a writer
the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is kept

parts.note: every other letter of the word, the first and third

explanation.surface: A decent writer whom one bumps into often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Okay' reads like an adjective, but it is the verb meaning to approve.
explanation.definitionFit: To okay a plan is to give it official approval, which is to sanction it; both are verbs.

clue.text: Beginning of the end for POTUS

indicators.note: a beginning is the start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
the rump is the hind end or backside

explanation.surface: A political jibe: the start of the end for the US president.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning of the end' reads as a set phrase, but it splits into the first letter of 'the' and a word for a backside.
explanation.definitionFit: POTUS is the acronym for President of the United States, an office held by Donald Trump.

indicators.note: at regular periods means every other letter is kept

parts.note: the even-numbered letters of the word

explanation.surface: Livestock mixing with each other from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: Neat is an archaic word for cattle, mostly found in crosswords and in 'neatsfoot oil'.
explanation.definitionFit: This old collective word for oxen and cows survives in compounds like neatherd, a herdsman.

indicators.note: stopping before the end means the final letter is lost

parts.note: the surname of the current UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A former government officer, the Chancellor knocking off work ahead of time.
explanation.walkthrough: Rachel Reeves became Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, the finance minister, in 2024; drop the S from Reeves.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeve was a medieval English local magistrate or manor overseer, hence an old official.

parts.note: surface reading: a figure promising something to come, like a vow about the nation's constitution
setter's reading: a song promising company on every stroll, a constitutional being a health-giving walk

explanation.surface: A political vow of backing for a country's founding document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is a song, not a figure; 'constitutional' is a walk taken for health. The song is a Rodgers and Hammerstein hit, the anthem of Liverpool FC.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's title promises companionship for every stroll, so it pledges support on future outings.

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
a petition is a formal request

explanation.surface: A very fair plea for a duplicate document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for 'reasonable', but it takes just the ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A repetition is a duplicate or reproduction of something already done, so it is a copy in that sense.

clue.text: Lewis for one is extremely louche

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Remarking that a man called Lewis is thoroughly disreputable.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis looks like a man's name, but it is the northern part of Lewis and Harris in Scotland's Outer Hebrides.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis is an example of an island, which is the meaning of the answer; 'for one' signals the example.
